tasks: Run `nest new tasks-nest` and `nest g resource tasks`, then open every generated file and write a one-line comment at the top of each saying what it is responsible for.
Port `GET /tasks`, `GET /tasks/:id` and `POST /tasks` from task-manager-api into the Nest app, with the Supabase client supplied as a provider — no top-level import of the client inside the service.
Delete `TasksService` from the module's `providers` array, boot the app, and read the resolution error out loud. Note which constructor index the `?` points at, then put it back.
Write one unit test for `TasksService` using `Test.createTestingModule` with a fake database provider, and confirm it runs with no network and no `.env`.
Instantiate the service twice — once through DI, once with `new` — and prove they hold separate state (see the trap).
Open your NestJS work project, pick one feature module, and draw its import graph on paper: which modules it imports, what it exports, who injects its service.
Count the lines of wiring in your Express `app.ts` versus the Nest `app.module.ts`, and count the files touched to add one endpoint in each. Write both numbers down.

quiz.q: Why does dependency injection make a service easier to unit test than the Express version that imports its Supabase client at the top of the file?
options: Because Nest services run in an isolated worker thread during tests
Because the service declares its collaborators as constructor parameters, so a test can hand it a fake instead of the real client
Because decorators disable side effects while `NODE_ENV` is `test`
Because Nest replaces all imports with mocks automatically
quiz.explain: A top-level import means the module constructs its own dependency the moment it loads. Declaring it in the constructor moves that decision outward, so a test supplies a stub and nothing real is touched.

quiz.q: `TasksModule` lists `TasksService` in `providers` but not in `exports`. `RemindersModule` imports `TasksModule` and injects `TasksService`. What happens?
options: It works — `providers` is enough for other modules to inject it
It works at runtime but the type is `any`
The app fails to start with a dependency resolution error naming the unsatisfied constructor argument
The container silently creates a second instance for RemindersModule
quiz.explain: `providers` makes a class injectable inside its own module; `exports` is what publishes it to importers. A missing export is caught at boot, which is exactly the point of the module system.

quiz.q: How does Nest know at runtime that a constructor parameter should be resolved to `TasksService`, given TypeScript types are erased when compiled?
options: It parses the source file for type annotations at startup
`emitDecoratorMetadata` makes the compiler emit parameter types as metadata, which Nest reads via `reflect-metadata`
The provider name is matched by string against the parameter name
The `@Injectable()` decorator serializes the whole class into the module registry
quiz.explain: Decorators plus `emitDecoratorMetadata` write the design-time parameter types into metadata; `reflect-metadata` lets the container read them back. This is also why a broken tsconfig produces confusing injection failures.

quiz.q: You call `new TasksService(db)` in a script instead of injecting it. The service keeps an in-memory cache. What is the observable symptom?
options: A runtime error, because `@Injectable()` classes cannot be constructed manually
Nothing — the container detects and reuses the existing instance
Two instances with separate caches that disagree, with no error or warning anywhere
The app fails to start on the next boot
quiz.explain: Nest providers are singletons managed by the container. Constructing one by hand produces a second, unmanaged object with its own state — no error, just two sources of truth that drift.

trap.title: The service that exists twice
trap.content:
Your `TasksService` keeps a tiny in-memory counter of how many tasks were created this process. Add one, expose it on `GET /tasks/stats`, and confirm it climbs.

Now, somewhere else — a job handler, a script, a second controller — write `const svc = new TasksService(db)` instead of injecting it, and create tasks through that. Hit `/tasks/stats` again.

The number doesn't move. You built a second service with its own counter, and nothing warned you: no error, no log, no type complaint. Whatever state that class holds — a cache, a connection, a rate-limit bucket, a debounce timer — now exists twice and disagrees with itself. This is the failure mode behind your own rule that services are injectable and never `new`ed, and it is almost impossible to debug after the fact, because the code looks correct on every line.

tasks: Reproduce the mass-assignment trap end to end, then close it with `whitelist: true` and `forbidNonWhitelisted: true` and watch the same request become a 400.
Convert two of your Zod schemas into class-validator DTOs, and write down for each one which tool you'd rather maintain and why.

Add a response DTO with `@Exclude()` on a sensitive field, return a plain database row from the controller, and confirm the field still leaks. Fix it with `plainToInstance` and add a test asserting the field is absent.
Register a global auth guard through the `APP_GUARD` token, add a `@Public()` decorator, then add a new route with no decorators and confirm it returns 401 rather than 200.
Write an exception filter producing one error envelope, throw `NotFoundException` from a service, and verify no stack trace appears in the response body when `NODE_ENV` is production.
Add a `ConfigModule` validation schema, remove one required variable, and confirm the process exits at boot instead of failing on a request.
Write one unit test with `Test.createTestingModule` and a mocked provider, plus one supertest e2e test asserting 401 on a protected route and 400 on a body carrying an undeclared field.

Audit your NestJS work project: where the global `ValidationPipe` is configured and whether `whitelist` is on, whether route protection defaults to open or closed, and whether the error filter can ever serialize a stack trace. Write the findings down.

quiz.q: What is the correct order in which Nest runs these for an incoming request?
options: pipe, guard, middleware, handler, interceptor, filter
middleware, guard, interceptor (before), pipe, handler, interceptor (after), filter
guard, middleware, pipe, interceptor, handler, filter
middleware, pipe, guard, handler, filter, interceptor
quiz.explain: Middleware runs first with no handler context, then guards decide access, then interceptors wrap the call, then pipes transform each argument, then the handler runs. Exception filters catch whatever is thrown along the way.

quiz.q: Your DTO declares only `title`. A request body includes `title` and `isAdmin`, and the global `ValidationPipe` has `transform: true` but no `whitelist`. What reaches your service?
options: Only `title` — undeclared keys are always dropped
Both keys, and the request succeeds
Nothing — the request is rejected with a 400
Both keys, but `isAdmin` is coerced to a string
quiz.explain: Without `whitelist: true`, validation only checks the fields it knows about and forwards the rest untouched. `whitelist` strips undeclared keys; `forbidNonWhitelisted` rejects the request instead.

quiz.q: You need a check that reads route metadata to decide whether the caller may proceed, and it needs to inject a service. Which slot, registered how?
options: Middleware, applied in `configure()` on the module
A guard registered with `app.useGlobalGuards(new MyGuard())`
A guard provided under the `APP_GUARD` token so the container can inject its dependencies
An interceptor registered globally in `main.ts`
quiz.explain: Only guards get an `ExecutionContext` with route metadata, and only a guard registered as a provider (via `APP_GUARD`) participates in DI. A guard constructed by hand in `main.ts` cannot inject anything.

quiz.q: A response DTO marks `passwordHash` with `@Exclude()`, `ClassSerializerInterceptor` is global, and yet the hash appears in the JSON. Why?
options: `@Exclude()` only applies to request bodies, not responses
The controller returned a plain object from the ORM, not an instance of the DTO class, so there were no decorators to apply
The interceptor runs before the handler and so never sees the value
`@Exclude()` requires `whitelist: true` on the ValidationPipe
quiz.explain: class-transformer works off metadata attached to a class. A plain row is just an object, so serialization has nothing to act on — construct the DTO instance (for example with `plainToInstance`) before returning it.

quiz.q: Why is a global auth guard with a `@Public()` opt-out safer than putting `@UseGuards(JwtAuthGuard)` on each route?
options: Global guards are faster because they are compiled once
Per-route guards cannot read route metadata
Because forgetting the decorator leaves a route locked and someone reports it, instead of leaving it open and nobody noticing
Because `@Public()` also disables rate limiting where it isn't needed
quiz.explain: The default matters more than the mechanism. Default-closed turns an omission into a visible 401; default-open turns the same omission into an unauthenticated endpoint that no one is looking for.

trap.title: The 201 that made an admin
trap.content:
Add a `role` column to your users table, defaulting to `"user"`. Write a signup endpoint whose DTO declares only `email` and `password`, and whose service passes the DTO straight to the insert. Register the global `ValidationPipe` with `transform: true` but **without** `whitelist`.

Now post this:

```json
{ "email": "attacker@example.com", "password": "hunter2", "role": "admin" }
```

Read the response: `201 Created`, no warning anywhere. Then read the row. `role` is `admin`.

Sit with the fact that your validator ran, passed, and reported success. It confirmed the two fields it knew about and forwarded everything else untouched. Now add `whitelist: true`, repeat the request, and watch the extra key vanish before the service is called. Add `forbidNonWhitelisted: true` and watch the same request become a 400. Then write the e2e test that fails if either flag is ever removed — that test is the only thing standing between this bug and its second appearance.

sq-13.content:
## The problem

Opening a mature NestJS codebase feels like reading a language where you know every word and no sentences. Eleven decorators sit above one method. A controller lives four folders from the module that lists it. Something called a repository module exports a repository, and neither is where you'd look. Two days in you still navigate by full-text search, which means you can't review a pull request in it with any confidence.

## The idea

The cure isn't more reading. It's having built the same thing once, in a shape you chose — after that, someone else's structure reads as *decisions*, and you can tell which were deliberate.

So port, don't rewrite. Freeze the Task Manager's behaviour: same endpoints, same tables, same response bodies. Only the shape changes. That isolates the variable, so what you feel at the end is NestJS and not new requirements.

## In practice

1. `nest new task-manager-nest`, then `ConfigModule.forRoot` with a schema covering every variable the Express app reads. Boot with one missing and confirm the process dies.
2. A `SupabaseModule` providing the client as an exported provider. Nothing else imports `@supabase/supabase-js` directly.
3. `nest g resource tasks`, then move `list`, `getById`, `create`, `update`, `delete` into `TasksService` — logic unchanged, `db` arriving through the constructor.
4. Zod schemas become DTOs with class-validator decorators, behind a global `ValidationPipe` with `whitelist: true` and `forbidNonWhitelisted: true`.
5. Response DTOs with `@Exclude()` on anything the client has no business seeing, plus `ClassSerializerInterceptor`.
6. A global `JwtAuthGuard` via the `APP_GUARD` token, with `@Public()` on health and login only.
7. One exception filter for the whole error envelope, with `NotFoundException` and `ForbiddenException` thrown from services.
8. Repeat for categories, and time yourself. The second resource is the point — it's where the per-feature cost drops.
9. Unit-test `TasksService` with a fake provider and no network, then e2e with supertest: 401 unauthenticated, 400 on an undeclared field.

## In your world

Now open your NestJS work project's `src/` and name each thing you just built. Per-feature folders holding controller, service, DTOs, repository. A `common/` tree with auth guards, error filters, response interceptors, pagination pipes. A router layer grouping features by prefix and audience. A `configs/` folder plus an env schema that fails at boot. Where its choices differ from yours — a repository layer wrapping the ODM, one decorator composing guard, policy and Swagger — ask what problem at that scale bought them. That question is your review voice.

## Watch out

- **A per-request database handle can't be a singleton.** If the client carries the caller's identity so row-level security applies, a module-scoped provider hands one user's handle to every request. Use a factory the service calls per request, or a deliberately request-scoped provider.
- **Don't copy a boilerplate's depth into a five-endpoint app.** Its layers exist for forty modules and ten contributors; at your size they are ceremony.
- **Port the behaviour, not the bugs.** Anything you can't explain while moving it should be fixed in the Express version first, with a test.
tasks: Port the tasks and categories resources of task-manager-api into a fresh Nest app with identical endpoints and response bodies, and diff a few real responses against the Express app to prove nothing changed.

Register the global `ValidationPipe` with `whitelist: true` and `forbidNonWhitelisted: true`, a global `JwtAuthGuard` via `APP_GUARD` with `@Public()` on health and login, and one exception filter for the whole app.
Write unit tests for both services with fake providers, plus supertest e2e tests covering 401 on a protected route, 404 from a typed exception, and 400 on an undeclared body field.
Time how long the second resource took versus the first, and write one paragraph on where the time went.

Read your NestJS work project's `src/` tree top to bottom and name, for each folder, which pattern from this port it corresponds to. List the three choices it makes that yours does not, and what scale would justify each.

quiz.q: Why port the Task Manager instead of building a new app in Nest?
options: Because Nest can generate a module automatically from Express routes
Because holding the behaviour constant means everything unfamiliar you feel is the framework, not new requirements
Because the Express version's tests transfer without modification
Because Nest requires an existing OpenAPI document to scaffold from
quiz.explain: Changing one variable at a time is the whole method. Same endpoints and same data means the only difference you experience is structural.

quiz.q: Your Supabase client carries the caller's JWT so row-level security applies. What is wrong with providing it as a normal module-scoped provider?
options: Nothing — Nest recreates providers per request by default
It is a singleton, so one user's authenticated handle would be shared across every request
Supabase clients cannot be used inside a DI container
It forces every consuming module to become request-scoped
quiz.explain: Providers are singletons unless you say otherwise. A handle that carries identity must be created per request — via a factory the service calls, or a deliberately request-scoped provider.

quiz.q: After the port, which patterns should you expect to recognize in a mature NestJS boilerplate's `src/`?
options: Per-feature modules with controller, service, DTOs and repository; a shared tree for guards, filters and interceptors; and config validated at boot
A single flat routes folder with one file per endpoint
Controllers containing the database queries, with services reserved for background jobs
One module per database table, with no shared code
quiz.explain: That is the shape Nest pushes you toward and the shape you just built by hand — which is why a large boilerplate should now read as decisions rather than noise.
